title: Two-beat versus four-beat rhythm sections
summary: Heavy four-beat drumming, Celestin's band, and the lost light two-beat style.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: Yeah, contrary to a lot of, to many people's opinion, we call it two beat, two four Dixieland music. It's associated with that. And the thing that surprised me the most is that these guys, for the most part, lay down a heavy four beat rhythm, you see. Just a punching style, you know, just a pounding style. And one of the few, a few musicians that I work with, I got to know very well, that had a light two beat style was Ray Badouk, Monk Hazel, you see. But for the most part, take Paul Barberin, you know, he laid down the hardest four beat driving style, and it would just pound right ahead like a herd of elephants, you see. And so did most of these drummers that played for us. Of course, Freddie Coleman is relatively a new drummer. He worked here a couple of years for us. We made a few record albums together. He's primarily a big band drummer, and he's more of the modern school, but he's capable of playing any style, any style of drum. But the rhythm section did amaze me. When Celestan was in here, let's see, who was on banjo for Celestan? Is that guy probably French? Must have been, yeah.
The guy that calls himself now probably French, I can't remember. He's the leader of the band, which has called itself the Celestan Band. I'm not sure whether he was playing for them then, maybe.

I don't know. I'd have to look up some pictures. We managed to keep some pictures, which I should have taken more of, because, believe me, they're treasured. And, uh, Celestan would be up there playing with these high, high-button shoes, and, uh, the band would be just driving. It sounded like a herd of elephants going down the street with a banjo and the piano playing four. Four, now, no two-beat on the piano rhythm, but just a straight-four drive, you know? And it had a tremendous, exciting effect. And it was a little bogey and a little heavy, and it wasn't a light thing, you know, sort of being a light thing. But it was a savage drive, a pounding drive, you know? And that's the first thing that, uh, I said, I wonder what happened to the two-beat light Dixieland? Like, .
